Explain that the emergency department must treat the client whatever the client can pay
Explain that the client can enroll in Medicare because hypertension is a chronic disease
questions.rationale:
For a client who can't afford care, the best first step is a referral to the social worker (or case manager). They can look at every option at once, such as marketplace plans the client may qualify for even when Medicaid says no, sliding-scale clinics, and drug-assistance programs, before the client stops the medication.

Sliding-scale clinics are a good resource, and the social worker may suggest one, but a list covers only part of the problem, which makes it the second-best choice. The emergency department must screen and stabilize emergencies whatever a client can pay (EMTALA), but it isn't a place for ongoing blood pressure care. Medicare covers people 65 and older and some people with disabilities or end-stage kidney disease, not every adult with a chronic illness.

Takeaway: A client who can't afford care: refer to the social worker or case manager first.

questions.stem: A nurse is listening to nursing students review levels of care before an exam. Which statement by a student needs correction?
options: “A 3-day hospital stay for IV antibiotics is secondary care.”
“Hospice is a kind of palliative care for clients near the end of life.”
“Palliative care starts once the client stops treatment aimed at a cure.”
“Weeks in an inpatient rehabilitation center after a stroke are tertiary care.”
questions.rationale:
This statement needs correction: palliative care can begin at any stage of a serious illness, while the client keeps receiving treatment aimed at a cure. Hospice is the kind of palliative care that comes when curative treatment stops, near the end of life.

The other statements are accurate. A 3-day hospital stay for IV antibiotics is secondary care: short-term care in a hospital. Hospice is palliative care for clients near the end of life (all hospice is palliative, but not all palliative care is hospice). Weeks in an inpatient rehabilitation center are tertiary care.

Takeaway: Palliative care relieves symptoms at any stage, with or without curative treatment. Hospice is palliative care at the end of life, when curative treatment has stopped.

questions.stem: A nurse on a surgical unit wonders whether the unit's routine of keeping clients NPO from midnight before afternoon surgery is still supported by evidence, and decides to start an evidence-based practice project. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Write a PICOT question comparing midnight fasting with clear liquids until 2 hours before surgery
Search CINAHL and PubMed for studies on how long clients should fast before surgery
Assess each client's thirst and hunger on the morning of surgery and report it to the surgeon
Review the unit's data on how long clients go without food or fluids before surgery
questions.rationale:
In this class, the steps of evidence-based practice start with Assess: identify the clinical problem, often from the unit's own data. Here, that means finding out how long clients actually go without food or fluids, and what problems it causes. The steps then go Ask (a PICOT question), Acquire (search), Appraise, Apply, and Evaluate.

Writing the PICOT question isn't the right answer: it's the first of Pearson's four steps, but those steps begin once the problem is known. In the class's six steps, it comes second. Searching CINAHL and PubMed is the third step, Acquire. Assessing each client's thirst and hunger is the nursing process's assessment, for one client's care plan; EBP's Assess looks at a problem across the unit.

Takeaway: EBP's first step is Assess (identify the clinical problem from the unit's data), then Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, and Evaluate. EBP assesses the problem; the nursing process assesses the client.

questions.stem: A nurse who recently moved to a new hospital sees that its procedure calls for flushing saline locks every 8 hours. The nurse's previous hospital flushed them every 12 hours, based on a recent study. A client's saline lock is due for its 8-hour flush. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Wait until 12 hours to flush the lock, since the newer evidence supports the longer interval
Ask the client which schedule they prefer, since preferences are part of evidence-based practice
Ask the charge nurse which schedule most of the unit's nurses follow, and follow that schedule
Flush the lock now, as the facility's policy requires, and bring the evidence to the practice council
questions.rationale:
A nurse follows the policy and procedure of the facility where they work, not a previous hospital's, even one based on good evidence. With evidence for a better way, the nurse keeps following the current policy and brings the evidence to the practice council (or the nurse manager or EBP committee), so it can be appraised and the policy changed for everyone.

Waiting until 12 hours isn't the right answer: the evidence may be sound, but changing practice on one's own puts the nurse outside the facility's standards. Asking the client misuses client preference: clients choose among the care options the facility offers, but they don't set its procedures. Doing what most nurses do trades the policy for habit.

Takeaway: Follow this facility's policy as written, and propose changes through its process, with the evidence.

questions.stem: Two months after a unit adopted evidence-based bedside handoff, several experienced nurses still give report at the desk. They say, “We've done it this way for years, and nothing bad has happened.” Which action should the nurse manager take?
options: Share the unit's own handoff-error data with the evidence, and ask these nurses to help plan the next steps
Remind the nurses that the new handoff is now policy, and that not following policy will go on their evaluations
Let each nurse choose the handoff method that works best until the whole staff agrees on one
Schedule a required class for these nurses on how to find, read, and judge research articles
questions.rationale:
These nurses' barrier is resistance to change: “We've always done it this way.” What helps is the unit's own data, alongside the evidence, so the problem feels real, and involving the nurses who resist in planning, so the change becomes theirs.

Pointing to policy and evaluations isn't the right answer: ordering or threatening staff gets compliance at best and doesn't change minds. Waiting until everyone agrees stalls the change. A class on judging research fixes a different barrier, lack of skill: these nurses aren't saying they can't read research, but that they see no reason to change.

Takeaway: Match the fix to the barrier. For resistance, share the unit's data with the evidence and involve staff early; for lack of time or skill, protected time, champions, and education.

questions.stem: A nurse on a medical unit for older adults wants evidence on preventing falls among the unit's hospitalized clients. Which source should the nurse rely on most?
options: A large randomized controlled trial of a fall-prevention program among nursing home residents
A systematic review of randomized trials of fall prevention in hospitalized older adults
A qualitative study of how hospitalized older adults feel about their risk of falling
A respected nurse expert's opinion article on preventing falls in older adults
questions.rationale:
A systematic review of randomized controlled trials is the strongest level of evidence, and this one studied hospitalized older adults, the same kind of clients as the unit's. Strength and fit both point to it.

The large randomized controlled trial isn't the right answer: it's strong evidence (the next level down), but it studied nursing home residents, whose setting and risks differ. Appraising evidence includes asking whether it fits your clients. The qualitative study describes how clients feel, not whether a program prevents falls. An expert's opinion is the weakest level of evidence.

Takeaway: Choose the strongest evidence that fits your clients: systematic reviews of randomized trials first, then single randomized trials, with weaker designs and opinion last.

questions.stem: Strong evidence supports walking on the day after abdominal surgery. On postoperative day 1, a client refuses to walk, saying, “My incision hurts too much, and I'm afraid it will open.” Which action by the nurse best reflects evidence-based practice?
options: Explain that research shows walking prevents complications, and help the client walk now as the protocol requires
Document the refusal and skip walking today, since respecting the client's choice comes first
Check the incision, reassure the client that it's intact, and let the client rest until tomorrow
Assess the pain, give the prescribed analgesic, teach splinting, and agree with the client on a time to walk
questions.rationale:
Evidence-based practice combines the best evidence (early walking prevents complications), the nurse's expertise (pain is what's keeping this client in bed, and pain control and splinting can fix that), and the client's preferences (agreeing on a time). So the nurse treats the pain, teaches splinting, and plans the walk with the client.

Walking the client now because the protocol requires it isn't the right answer: it follows the evidence but leaves out the client's preferences and the nurse's judgment about pain. Skipping the walk respects the refusal but drops the evidence, and the teaching that might change the client's mind. Checking the incision and letting the client rest starts with an assessment, but it puts off a proven intervention without treating the pain behind the refusal.

Takeaway: EBP isn't research alone: it's the evidence, plus the nurse's expertise, plus the client's preferences.

questions.stem: A caller says she is a client's daughter and correctly gives the client's date of birth and room number. She asks how her mother's surgery went. The client is awake and alert. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the daughter a short update, since she knew the client's date of birth and room number
Tell the daughter that the hospital gives updates to family in person, at the bedside
Transfer the call to the surgeon, who decides what family members may be told
Check whether the client has authorized sharing with the daughter, and if not, ask the client
questions.rationale:
The client decides who may receive information. Knowing the client's date of birth and room number doesn't show that a caller is authorized: anyone who knows the client could know them. So the nurse checks for the client's authorization (a release or a privacy code), and since the client is awake and alert, can simply ask.

Giving a short update isn't the right answer: the caller sounds legitimate, but identifiers aren't permission. There's no rule that updates must be given in person: an authorized person can be told by phone. The surgeon doesn't decide who may know; the client does.

Takeaway: Before sharing anything, confirm that the client has authorized this person. Identifiers prove nothing about permission.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a well-known local news anchor on a medical unit. Which actions by the nurse protect the client's confidentiality?
options: Turning the computer screen toward the wall before stepping into another client's room
Logging off the computer before stepping into another client's room
Using the client's first name, without the last name, when discussing care in the hallway
Confirming that the client has authorized a caller before giving any update
Shredding the printed handoff sheet at the end of the shift
Closing the door and speaking quietly before discussing the client's care with the client
questions.rationale:
Logging off before leaving the computer, confirming the client's authorization before giving any update, shredding the handoff sheet, and closing the door and speaking quietly all protect the client's information.

Turning the screen toward the wall isn't the right answer: it hides the screen, but anyone can turn it back and use the open record. The nurse must log off or lock it. A first name in the hallway still identifies a well-known client, and care isn't discussed in hallways at all.

Takeaway: Log off, verify authorization, shred paper with client information, and keep conversations about care to private places.

questions.stem: A nurse is writing a focus (DAR) note about a client who is anxious the evening before surgery. Which statement belongs in the A section of the note?
options: Anxiety related to the upcoming surgery, as shown by pacing and repeated questions
Pacing in the room; asks, “What if I don't wake up?” Heart rate 104/min.
Explained what to expect, taught slow breathing, and stayed with the client
States feeling calmer after the teaching; heart rate 88/min.
questions.rationale:
In focus charting (DAR), A stands for Action: what the nurse did. Explaining what to expect, teaching slow breathing, and staying with the client are actions.

“Anxiety related to the upcoming surgery” isn't the right answer, even though A means Assessment in a SOAP note. That nursing-diagnosis statement fits SOAP's A or PIE's P, never DAR's A. Pacing and the client's question are Data (D). Feeling calmer, with a slower heart rate, is the Response (R).

Takeaway: DAR: Data (what you saw and heard), Action (what you did), Response (how the client responded). A is Assessment only in SOAP.

questions.stem: At 1600, a nurse realizes two things: a dressing change done at 1100 was never charted, and the 1400 vital signs were charted in the wrong client's paper record. Which actions should the nurse take?
options: Write a new entry labeled “late entry,” with the current time, stating that the dressing was changed at 1100
Add the dressing change in the space after the 1000 entry, so the notes stay in time order
Cover the vital signs in the wrong record with correction tape, to protect the other client's privacy
Draw a single line through the vital signs in the wrong record, and write “error” with initials, date, and time
Chart the vital signs in the correct client's record as a late entry, with the time they were taken
Write “incident report filed” next to the corrected entry, so reviewers know the error was reported
questions.rationale:
The forgotten dressing change gets a new entry labeled “late entry,” written at the current time and stating when the care was done. The vital signs in the wrong record get a single line, “error,” and the nurse's initials, date, and time, leaving them readable. Then the vital signs are charted in the correct client's record, as a late entry with the time they were taken.

Covering the entry with correction tape isn't the right answer. It seems to protect the other client's privacy, but a record is never obscured: the single line keeps it honest and legal. Squeezing the note into the space after 1000 makes it look as if it was written then, which falsifies the record. “Incident report filed” never goes in the chart: the report is a confidential QI tool.

Takeaway: Late entries are labeled and written at the current time; errors get a single line, “error,” initials, date, and time. Nothing is squeezed in, covered up, or labeled as an incident in the chart.

questions.stem: When a nurse scans a vial of IV hydromorphone, the scanner warns that the ordered dose is above the safe range. The nurse holds the dose and calls the pharmacist, who confirms that the order was written for 10 times the intended dose. The provider corrects the order before any is given. Which statement about this event is accurate?
options: It is a near miss, and the nurse completes an incident report so the ordering process can be reviewed
It is a near miss, and since the client wasn't harmed, a report isn't needed
It is a medication error, because a wrong dose was ordered, and the nurse completes an incident report
It is an adverse drug event, and the nurse writes a description of it in the client's medical record
questions.rationale:
The 10-fold order was caught before any of it reached the client, which makes it a near miss, a good catch. Near misses still get an incident report, so the QI team can find out how a 10-fold order got written and fix the process for everyone.

No report, since no one was harmed, isn't the right answer: near misses show where the system is weak before someone is hurt, which is exactly why they're reported. A medication error is a mistake that reaches the client. An adverse drug event is harm from exposure to a medication, and none was given; and the event doesn't belong in the medical record.

Takeaway: Caught before it reached the client: a near miss. Reached the client: an error. Death or serious harm: a sentinel event. Report them all, and keep the reports out of the chart.

questions.stem: A QI team will test a new turning schedule to prevent pressure injuries on one unit, using the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle. Which activities belong in the Plan phase?
options: Using the turning schedule on the unit for 8 weeks
Recording the unit's pressure-injury rate for the past 6 months
Comparing the rate during the test with the prediction
Predicting that the rate will fall by 30% within 8 weeks
Adding the turning schedule to the hospital's skin-care policy
Deciding who will collect the turning data, and how
questions.rationale:
The Plan phase prepares the test: baseline data (the past 6 months' rate), a prediction (a 30% drop in 8 weeks), and who will collect the data, and how.

Using the schedule for 8 weeks is the Do phase, the small-scale test. Comparing the rate with the prediction is the Study phase. Adding the schedule to the hospital's policy is the Act phase, once the test shows it works.

Takeaway: Plan: baseline data, a goal and a prediction, who does what. Do: test it small. Study: compare the results with the prediction. Act: adopt, adapt, or abandon.

questions.stem: A unit's QI team reviewed 6 months of its data on catheter-associated urinary tract infections, found that its rate is higher than those of the best units in its health system, and chose this as the area to improve. Which step should the team take next?
options: Start a catheter-removal reminder in the electronic record across the hospital
Compare the unit's infection rate once more with the rates of the best units in the system
Measure whether the unit's infection rate has dropped since the last quarter
Find out which practices the best-performing units use that lead to fewer infections
questions.rationale:
The team has already done the first three steps of the QI process: it analyzed its data, compared itself with the best units (benchmarking), and chose an area to improve. Next comes research: what do the best performers do that leads to fewer infections?

Starting a reminder across the hospital isn't the right answer: it puts a change in place before the team knows what works; changes come in step 5. Comparing with the best units again repeats step 2. Measuring whether the rate dropped is step 6, which follows a change.

Takeaway: The QI process: analyze current care, compare with the leaders, identify the area, research what works, put changes in place, analyze the outcomes, and repeat.

questions.stem: A medical unit's quarterly report compares its results with the national benchmark for similar units. For each measure, a lower number is better. Which result should the unit's nursing QI council work on first?
options: Time for lab results to come back: 70 minutes (benchmark 45)
Falls with injury: 1.4 per 1,000 client days (benchmark 0.9)
Catheter-associated urinary tract infections: 0.8 per 1,000 catheter days (benchmark 1.2)
Elective surgeries canceled: 12 per month (benchmark 8)
questions.rationale:
Falls with injury are a nurse-sensitive indicator (nursing care directly affects them), and the unit's rate is worse than the benchmark. Both point the nursing QI council to it.

Catheter-associated infections aren't the right answer: they're nurse-sensitive too, but this unit is better than the benchmark. Lab turnaround time and canceled surgeries are worse than their benchmarks, but they depend on the lab and the surgical schedule, not on nursing care, so they aren't nurse-sensitive.

Takeaway: A nursing QI council works on nurse-sensitive indicators (falls, pressure injuries, CAUTI, CLABSI, staffing) that are worse than their benchmarks.

questions.stem: A client on a surgical unit received 10 times the prescribed dose of IV heparin and developed serious bleeding. The hospital begins a root cause analysis. Which questions should the team ask?
options: Which nurse gave the dose, and has that nurse made medication errors before?
Were two strengths of heparin stored in the same bin?
Was the nurse interrupted, or working an extra shift, during the medication pass?
Was the family satisfied with how the staff explained the event?
Did the infusion pump's drug library have a dose limit for heparin?
Was the order written clearly, with the dose and its units?
questions.rationale:
A root cause analysis looks at everything in the system that let the error happen: storage (two strengths in one bin invite a mix-up), workload and interruptions, equipment (a drug library dose limit could have stopped the overdose), and communication (an unclear order).

Which nurse gave the dose, and whether that nurse made errors before, isn't the right answer: it sounds like fact-finding, but it aims at one person. An RCA looks for system causes, and blame makes staff stop reporting. The family's satisfaction with the explanation matters for disclosure, but it isn't a cause of the error.

Takeaway: An RCA asks what in the system let an error happen (storage, staffing, interruptions, equipment, communication, policies, training), never who to blame.

questions.stem: A nurse manager pulls 20 records of clients who received an opioid and finds that a pain reassessment within 1 hour was documented in 12 of them, although policy requires it every time. Which action should the manager take next?
options: Share the results, add an EHR reminder for reassessment, and audit again in a month
Ask the nurses who skipped the reassessments to add them to those records now
Complete an incident report for each of the 8 records, send them to risk management, and track the trend
Start a root cause analysis to find out why the 8 reassessments were missed
questions.rationale:
A chart audit shows how well documentation follows policy. With reassessments missing in 8 of 20 records, the next steps are to share the results, fix the process (a reminder in the electronic record makes the right thing easy), and audit again to see whether it worked.

Asking nurses to add the missing reassessments now isn't the right answer: entries added to past shifts after an audit can't be trusted, and they hide the problem instead of fixing it. Incident reports each describe one unusual event, so filing 8 of them sounds thorough, but a documentation pattern found in an audit is improved through the QI process. A root cause analysis is for a serious event, like a sentinel event, not a documentation pattern.

Takeaway: After a chart audit: share the results, improve the process, and audit again. Don't add missing entries to past shifts.

questions.stem: A client's employer health plan, which isn't exempt from the parity law, requires prior authorization before every outpatient therapy visit for depression, but none for outpatient visits for diabetes. The client asks whether this is allowed. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “No. The plan can't require approval for therapy visits unless it does for similar medical visits.”
“Yes. The parity law covers copays and visit limits, but not rules like prior authorization.”
“No. Plans can't require prior authorization for mental health care, whatever their medical rules.”
“Yes. The parity law protects substance use treatment, not therapy for depression.”
questions.rationale:
The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act says a plan's mental health and substance use benefits can't be more restrictive than its medical benefits. That covers money rules, like copays and deductibles, and treatment rules, like visit limits and prior authorization. Requiring approval for every therapy visit but not for diabetes visits is a stricter rule for mental health care, so it isn't allowed.

“Copays and visit limits, but not prior authorization” isn't the right answer: parity is usually explained with money examples, but it covers rules like prior authorization too. “Plans can't require prior authorization for mental health care” goes too far: parity doesn't ban the rule, it bans a stricter rule for mental health than for medical care. And the law covers both mental health and substance use care, so therapy for depression is included.

Takeaway: Parity means equal rules, not no rules: copays, deductibles, visit limits, and prior authorization for mental health and substance use care can't be stricter than for medical care.

questions.topic: HIPAA, PHI, FDA, and health literacy
questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing when a client's health information may be shared without the client's written authorization. Which situations allow it?
options: Telling the client's employer why the client missed work, when the employer calls
Giving report to the nurse who is taking over the client's care
Giving test results to the client's spouse, who is listed as the emergency contact
Sending the client's records to the client's insurer to bill for the stay
Reporting the client's new tuberculosis diagnosis to the local health department
Describing the client's unusual injury, without the client's name, in a nursing students' online group
questions.rationale:
HIPAA allows sharing without written authorization for treatment (report to the next nurse), payment (billing the insurer), and health care operations, and when the law requires it, like reporting tuberculosis to the health department.

The spouse listed as the emergency contact isn't the right answer: being an emergency contact doesn't give the spouse permission to receive test results; the client decides that. The employer has no right to know why the client missed work. A post in an online group without the client's name is still a breach: details like an unusual injury can identify the client, and client stories don't go online.

Takeaway: Without written authorization: treatment, payment, operations, and what the law requires (public health reports, abuse reports, court orders). Everyone else needs the client's permission.

questions.topic: HIPAA, PHI, FDA, and health literacy
questions.stem: During orientation, a new nurse asks which of these must be protected under HIPAA. Which item should the nurse identify as protected health information?
options: A comment in the elevator about “the teacher in room 412 who had a miscarriage”
A poster in the break room showing the unit's monthly rate of falls
A textbook case study about a client who has diabetes, using a made-up name and age
A research table of average blood pressures for 200 participants, with no names
questions.rationale:
Protected health information is health information that can identify a person, in any form, spoken too. A comment about “the teacher in room 412” and her miscarriage identifies her (a room number and a job) and links her to a diagnosis, so it's PHI, and saying it in an elevator is a breach.

A monthly fall rate on a poster has no identifiers. The textbook case with a made-up name isn't about a real person. The research table of averages, with no names, can't identify anyone. Thinking any health information is PHI is a mistake: it's PHI when it can identify someone.

Takeaway: PHI = health information + something that identifies the person, whether it's written, electronic, or spoken.

questions.topic: HIPAA, PHI, FDA, and health literacy
questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing federal agencies with nursing students. Which statement by a student indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “The FDA approves new drugs and medical devices as safe and effective before they're sold.”
“Nurses can report a serious reaction to a drug to the FDA through MedWatch.”
“The FDA sets the workplace rules that protect nurses from needlestick injuries.”
“The FDA can recall a drug or device that turns out to be unsafe.”
questions.rationale:
This statement needs more teaching: workplace rules that protect nurses, like the bloodborne pathogens and needlestick rules, come from OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, not the FDA.

The other statements are accurate. The FDA approves drugs and devices as safe and effective before they're sold, collects reports of adverse events through MedWatch, and can recall a drug or device that proves unsafe.

Takeaway: FDA: drugs, devices, recalls, MedWatch. OSHA: worker safety. CDC: infection control and public health. NIH: research.

questions.topic: HIPAA, PHI, FDA, and health literacy
questions.stem: A hospital's 30-day readmission rate for clients with heart failure is high. A review finds that many of these clients couldn't explain their medications or warning signs at discharge. Which policy change would best address the problem?
options: Require clients to sign a form stating that they understand their discharge instructions
Require teach-back, with plain-language instructions written at about a 6th-grade level
Give clients a complete printed copy of the discharge plan and each medication's full drug guide
Require nurses to ask, “Do you have any questions?” before each client leaves the unit
questions.rationale:
Clients who can't explain their medications or warning signs weren't taught in a way they could use. Teach-back (“Tell me in your own words how you'll take this”) shows what the client understood, and plain-language instructions at about a 6th-grade reading level make the material usable. Both are what health literacy policy calls for.

“Do you have any questions?” isn't the right answer: a client who doesn't understand often has no questions, and a yes or no proves nothing. A signed form proves the client signed, not that they understood. More printed material, like full drug guides, is harder to use for a client with low health literacy.

Takeaway: To know a client understood, have them teach it back, in plain language. A yes, a signature, or more paper proves nothing.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four entries documented during the shift. Which entry contains an abbreviation that needs correction?
options: 0800: Gave insulin glargine 20 units subcut.
0900: Gave furosemide 20 mg IV; voided 400 mL at 1000.
1000: Gave vitamin D 1,000 IU PO with breakfast.
1100: Gave enoxaparin 40 mg subcut in the abdomen.
questions.rationale:
IU (international units) is on The Joint Commission's Do-Not-Use list: it can be misread as IV or as 10. The entry should say “1,000 international units.”

The other entries are correct. “Units” is written out, subcut is the accepted way to write subcutaneous (SC, SQ, and sub q are the error-prone ones), and mL is right (cc is the one to avoid). “Subcut” isn't the right answer: some subcutaneous abbreviations are risky, but “subcut” is the safe form.

Takeaway: Do not use U, IU, QD, QOD, MS, MSO4, MgSO4, trailing zeros, or a missing leading zero. Write subcut, mL, and units.

questions.topic: Med math: fill in the blank
questions.stem: From 0700 to 1500, a client drank 3/4 of an 8-oz carton of milk, ate scrambled eggs and a slice of toast, had 1 cup of ice chips, and drank 120 mL of water with medications. The client also received a 50-mL IV antibiotic piggyback and two 10-mL saline flushes. What is the client's total intake for the shift?
questions.rationale:
Total intake counts every fluid the client took in, by mouth and by IV. Change each item to mL, then add:

Milk: 8 oz × 30 = 240 mL, and the client drank 3/4 of it: 240 × 3/4 = 180 mL.
Eggs and toast: solid food, 0 mL.
Ice chips: 1 cup = 240 mL of ice, which counts as half its volume: 120 mL.
Water with medications: 120 mL.
IV piggyback: 50 mL.
Flushes: 2 × 10 = 20 mL.

Total: 180 + 120 + 120 + 50 + 20 = 490 mL. The usual mistakes: counting the whole carton (550), counting the ice chips at full volume (610), or leaving out the IV fluids (420).

Takeaway: Count what was actually consumed, ice chips at half their volume, no solid food, and IV fluids, piggybacks, and flushes in the total intake.

questions.topic: Med math: fill in the blank
questions.stem: A provider prescribes cefazolin 1 g in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV, to infuse over 45 minutes. The nurse will use an infusion pump. At how many mL/hr should the nurse set the pump?
questions.rationale:
An infusion pump runs in mL per hour, so change the minutes to hours first: 45 minutes ÷ 60 = 0.75 hour. Then divide the volume by the time: 100 mL ÷ 0.75 hr = 133.33 mL/hr, which rounds to 133 mL/hr.

The usual mistake is dividing by 45 (about 2) or multiplying by it, forgetting that the pump's rate is per hour. Another way to set it up: 100 mL ÷ 45 min × 60 min/hr = 133 mL/hr.

Takeaway: mL/hr = total mL ÷ hours. When the time is in minutes, change it to hours first (minutes ÷ 60).

questions.stem: A provider prescribes 500 mL of lactated Ringer's solution IV, to infuse over 4 hours. No pump is available, so the nurse will regulate the infusion by gravity, using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. At how many drops per minute should the nurse set the infusion?
options: 8 gtt/min
31 gtt/min
125 gtt/min
1,875 gtt/min
questions.rationale:
For a gravity infusion, gtt/min = total mL × drop factor ÷ total minutes. The time is 4 hours × 60 = 240 minutes. So 500 × 15 ÷ 240 = 7,500 ÷ 240 = 31.25, and drops are rounded to a whole number: 31 gtt/min.

125 is the rate in mL per hour (500 ÷ 4), what a pump would be set to, not drops per minute. 1,875 comes from dividing by 4 hours instead of 240 minutes. 8 comes from dividing by the drop factor instead of multiplying by it.

Takeaway: Drops per minute = mL × drop factor ÷ minutes. Change hours to minutes, and round drops to a whole number.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's new medication orders. Which orders should the nurse clarify with the prescriber before carrying them out?
options: Morphine 2 mg IV q2h PRN
Furosemide 40 mg PO daily
Insulin lispro 4 U subcut AC
Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO
Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO BID
Docusate sodium 100 PO at bedtime
questions.rationale:
A complete order has the drug, the dose (number and unit), the route, and when to give it, and a PRN order also says why. Morphine 2 mg IV q2h PRN doesn't say what it's for. Insulin lispro 4 U uses U, which can be misread as 0 or 4 (40 or 44 units). Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO doesn't say how often. Docusate sodium 100 PO has no unit for the dose. The nurse clarifies all four before giving them, and never fills in the missing piece.

Furosemide 40 mg PO daily and potassium chloride 20 mEq PO BID each have a drug, a dose with its unit, a route, and a time.

Takeaway: Check every order for the drug, the dose (number and unit), the route, and the time, plus the reason for a PRN, and for Do-Not-Use abbreviations. Clarify anything missing; never guess.
